descr:
Smarter 'Prime' Function

In the slides, there's an exercise to implement this function to practice writing loops recursively: is_prime function:

let rec is_prime i n =
  if i = n then true
  else if n mod i == 0 then false
  else is_prime (i+1) n
(* Call the function as is_prime 2 n,
   so that i always starts at 2. *)

But this function works too hard - it could stop at the square root of n instead of counting all the way up to n. The challenge is that we have to do it right. It makes the program worse if we are not careful to only call sqrt once.

In this exercise, we are demonstrating a new feature of LearnOCaml: hidden functions. We've provided a sqrt function, similar to the one from the other associated exercise from the slides. However, this sqrt function crashes if you use it more than once. The way it does that is a bit complex, so to avoid confusion, we've hidden the definition of the function. However you can still use it! Its type is sqrt : int -> int.

Complete the implementation of is_prime using any recursive style you want. Assume that n >= 2. You must call sqrt exactly once.

As a hint; this time, a local helper function is required - but you also need a local value.

Aside

So-called "primality tests" have been a subject of study for as long as mathematicians have been thinking about prime numbers. But only recently, in 2002, was it proven that there are primality tests which remain fast even when n becomes gigantic. Most tests suffer from the fact that division itself becomes much slower as n grows.

It's remains an area of research - we know that there are fast algorithms, but no one has been able to prove that there are not faster algorithms.

If this field of complexity interests you, it's incredibly rich and there's a lot that can be learned and solved. For primes, I'd suggest starting with the Seive of Atkins, and then exploring the "AKS Primality Test" published in 2002.
